abstract: Group-living animals rely on effective cohesion and coordination mechanisms to move collectively, emerging from the combination or confrontation of individual spatial knowledge. This knowledge is often asymmetrically distributed among group members, as it results from both individual experience and collective processes. However, the cohesive nature of such species makes it difficult to disentangle what individuals know on their own from how such information is incorporated into collective movement decisions. To better understand this, we investigated solitary homing in meerkats (Suricata suricatta) in their natural habitat, the Kalahari Desert, South Africa. We captured 20 adult meerkats from five wild groups during foraging and released them 1.5 km away from their group within their territory. Using a combination of in situ observations and remote sensing technology, we characterised solo navigation by assessing behavioural profiles (exploration and cue-searching behaviour) across three homing phases, as well as navigational efficiency during relocation (path linearity and heading precision at start). Eighteen individuals (90%) left the release point, all of which successfully homed, and 70% re-joined their group on their own. Although individuals varied in how they searched for cues, relocation performance (orientation and navigation accuracy) was overall high. Inter-individual differences in relocation performance could not be explained by individual traits or experience. This suggests that daily life in a meerkat social group provides ample opportunities for spatial learning, enabling all group members to navigate independently. These findings provide a clearer understanding of the individual-level capacities that likely support collective movement and decision-making in meerkats.
